text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Thursday.

GERMANY - Bund futures are expected to remain stuck in their recent range on Friday after shrugging off a flurry of official pronouncements on European monetary union to dip in line with Treasuries on Thursday. The June Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 100.11, down 0.16 from Wednesday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilts suffered from a lack of news which left them drifting sideways in thin volume and awaiting U.S. retail sales and producer price data to inject some life into the market on Friday. The June long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 108-29/32, down 07/32 from Wednesday's settlement price.

FRANCE - Bond futures settled lower as the market consolidated after three days of gains. Weak U.S. Treasuries fail to inspire. Market looks to U.S. data due on Friday. The June notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 128.34, down 0.26 from Wednesday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian debt markets were lying low along with other bond markets, taking stock of the political situation in Italy. The June bond future on LIFFE was trading at 127.20, down 0.55 from Wednesday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasuries widened modest losses at mid-morning. The June Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 107-08/32, down 03/32 from Wednesday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 7.12 percent.

JAPAN - Key June 10-year Japanese government bond futures closed slightly firmer, while long-term cash bonds were weaker. In after hours trading the June future on LIFFE was trading at 126.91, down 0.04 from Wednesday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
EUROBONDS - Dollar issuance led the way in the primary market as the U.S. currency continued to ride high ahead of key economic data.

L-Bank launched its expected $500 million five-year bond at an indicated 10 basis points yield spread via Goldman Sachs International and Morgan Stanley International. Bankers close to the deal said it had been extremely well received.
